newsitem.title: CHINA: China B share markets soar on "rubbish stocks".
newsitem.headline: China B share markets soar on "rubbish stocks".

text.p: China's two B share markets soared on Monday, with the Shanghai index hitting a three-year high thanks to an inflow of domestic investors targetting so-called "rubbish stocks", brokers said.
Shanghai's B share index surged 8.641 points or 12.96 percent to end at a 1996 closing high of 75.331 points, with volume of 91.3 million shares, the biggest this year, worth just under $34 million.

The Shenzhen B index surged 17.35 points, or 9.60 percent, to 198.14, its highest closing level since November 1993, with turnover rising to HK$779.22 million (US$99.9 million), also the highest since late 1993.
"Most of the buyers today in Shanghai were domestic investors targetting 'rubbish stocks'," said one Chinese broker, referring to low-priced, unpopular share issues.
"This is the same strategy they have used in the A share market, targetting good-quality stocks first and then the poor ones, which foreign investors will not buy," he added.
Shanghai Lianhua Fibre, a poorly-regarded firm which makes yarn and polyester, was the star on bargain-hunting, surging $0.074 or 44.04 percent to $0.242, on volume of 3.6 million shares.
"With the rise of the A share market, the discount between A shares of companies and their B share equivalent widened, making the B shares more attractive," the broker said.

A second Chinese broker said it was clear the regulators had given up attempts to enforce a ban on mainland Chinese buying foreign currency B shares which are legally reserved for investors outside China.

"The regulators have published the ban but not produced specific regulations to enforce it," he said. "Another bullish factor was rumours that the government will announce measures to boost the market and pick better-quality firms for listing."
In Shenzhen, the market was also dominated by Chinese investors attracted by its recent rises, brokers said.
Trading has become increasingly speculative and will become more volatile in the coming sessions, they said.
"The market's sharp gains over the past month have been attracting more and more investors, especially mainland Chinese," said a broker at China Southern Securities.
"Securities regulators may act to cool the excessively bullish sentiment, by such measures as tightening controls on buying by domestic investors," he said.
